15   3.      SCOPE

16           The protections conferred by this Stipulated Protective Order cover not only Protected Ma-

17   terial, as defined above and including any Protected Material produced or disclosed in this matter

18   prior to the entry of this Order, but also (1) any information copied or extracted from Protected

19   Material; (2) all copies, excerpts, summaries, or compilations of Protected Material; and (3) any

20   testimony, conversations, or presentations by Parties or their Counsel that might reveal Protected

21   Material. However, the protections conferred by this Stipulated Protective Order do not cover the

22   following information: (a) any information that is in the public domain at the time of disclosure to

23   a Receiving Party or becomes part of the public domain after its disclosure to a Receiving Party as

24   a result of publication not involving a violation of this Order, including becoming part of the public

25   record through trial or otherwise; and (b) any information known to the Receiving Party prior to

4            Even after final disposition of this litigation, the confidentiality obligations imposed by this

5    Order remain in effect until a Designating Party agrees otherwise in writing or a court order oth-

6    erwise directs. Final disposition will be deemed to be the later of (1) dismissal of all claims and

7    defenses in this action, with or without prejudice; and (2) final judgment herein after the comple-

9    the time limits for filing any motions or applications for extension of time pursuant to applicable

10   law and the time limits for filing a petition for writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of the United

11   States, if applicable.

13           5.1     Exercise of Restraint and Care in Designating Material for Protection. Each Party

14   or Non-Party that designates Disclosure or Discovery Material for protection under this Order must

15   take care to limit any such designation to specific material that qualifies under the appropriate

16   standards, including Local Civil Rule 79-5 and Rules 1, 26(b)(5), 26(c), 34(b)(2) and 37 of the

17   Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

18           If it comes to a Designating Party’s attention that Disclosure or Discovery Material that it

19   designated for protection does not qualify for protection at all or does not qualify for the level of

20   protection initially asserted, that Designating Party must promptly notify all other Parties that it is

21   withdrawing or revising the designation.

22           5.2     Manner and Timing of Designations. Except as otherwise provided in this Stipu-

23   lated Protective Order (see, e.g., Section 5.2(b) below), or as otherwise stipulated or ordered, Dis-

24   closure or Discovery Material that qualifies for protection under this Stipulated Protective Order

25   must be clearly so designated before the material is disclosed or produced.

4    6.     CHALLENGING CONFIDENTIALITY DESIGNATIONS

5           6.1     Timing of Challenges. Any Party may challenge a designation of confidentiality

6    or non-designation at any time. Unless a prompt challenge to a Designating Party’s confidentiality

7    designation is necessary to avoid foreseeable, substantial unfairness, unnecessary economic bur-

8    dens, or a significant disruption or delay of the litigation, a Party does not waive its right to chal-

9    lenge a confidentiality designation by electing not to mount a challenge promptly after the original

10   designation is disclosed.

11          6.2     Meet and Confer. The Challenging Party shall initiate the dispute resolution pro-

12   cess by providing written notice of each designation it is challenging and describing the basis for

13   the challenge. To avoid ambiguity as to whether a challenge has been made, the written notice

14   must recite that the challenge to confidentiality is being made in accordance with this specific

15   paragraph of the Stipulated Protective Order.

16          The Designating Party shall have an opportunity to respond in writing, and must do so

17   within 7 calendar days of a challenge being made, unless otherwise agreed. If a dispute remains,

18   the Parties shall attempt to resolve the challenge in good faith and shall meet and confer in person

19   or by phone or videoconference (other forms of communication are not sufficient) within 5 calen-

20   dar days of the date of service of the Designating Party’s written response, unless otherwise agreed.

21   In conferring, the Challenging Party must explain the basis for its belief that the confidentiality

22   designation was not proper and must give the Designating Party an opportunity to review the des-

23   ignated material, to reconsider the circumstances, and, if no change in designation is offered, to

24   explain the basis for the chosen designation. A Challenging Party may proceed to the next stage

25   of the challenge process only if it has engaged in this meet and confer process first.

26          6.3     Judicial Intervention. If the Parties cannot resolve a challenge without court inter-

puted changes, the Court orders as follows.

of any modifications to Meta’s competitor list. This clause will allow the Court to balance

the equities involved in adding a Meta competitor to the list mid-case, including the effects

Such a requirement may interfere with how the parties use material obtained outside discov-

ery. Rule 26 “does not authorize the court to limit use by a party of confidential information

Wright & Miller, Fed. Prac. & Proc. Civ. § 2043 (3d ed. Apr. 2026 update).

       3. Permitting Disclosure to Those with “Authority to Access”. Plaintiff proposes add-

ing to the list of persons with whom the parties may share protected material those “who had

access to or the authority to access or obtain” the material in the ordinary course of business.

Dkt. 77-3 § 7.3(h). The Model Order limits disclosure to persons who “possessed or knew

the information.” § 7.3(g). Plaintiff hasn’t persuaded the Court that its more expansive phras-

ing is warranted. The Court adopts Meta’s version of § 7.3(h), which tracks the Model Order.

       4. Patent Prosecution Bar. Meta hasn’t convinced the Court that a patent prosecution

bar is needed. Although Meta may need to produce source code, auction algorithms, and

other proprietary information, dkt. 77 at 5, the Model Order, as modified by the parties’

agreed-upon changes, should adequately protect that material from misuse. This isn’t a pa-

tent case, and Meta hasn’t identified anyone involved with the case who may prosecute re-

lated patents. If more concrete patent prosecution concerns later arise, Meta may move under

Rule 26 for a specific protective order if it can demonstrate good cause.

       5. Territorial Restrictions. Meta proposes that no protected material leave the United

States. The Model Order isn’t as restrictive, and Meta hasn’t demonstrated that tighter con-

trols are necessary. The Model Order already includes an optional “export control” provi-

sion. § 14.3. The parties shall use that provision, plus Plaintiff’s more narrowly tailored

restriction that no source code leave the United States.

fidential Information and/or Trade Secrets. See Dkt. 81-1 (Plaintiff’s redline); Dkt. 81-2 (De-

fendant’s redline). The Court endeavors to use the Model Protective Orders and so will re-

quire the parties to explain, in a joint statement to be filed by August 5, 2026, why their

proposed deviations are necessary.

       The parties also propose many changes to the Model ESI Discovery Order for Stand-

ard Litigation. See Dkt. 81-3 (Plaintiff’s redline); Dkt. 81-4 (Defendant’s redline). The Court

expects the parties to make changes to the Model ESI Discovery Orders, unlike the Model

Protective Orders, because the former are more like templates, with blank spaces in which

parties can include case-specific ESI agreements. The Court, then, won’t require the parties
     Case 3:25-cv-03281-CRB             Document 83       Filed 07/29/26      Page 2 of 2




to justify their jointly proposed changes to the Model ESI Order.

       The only dispute regarding the ESI Order is the deadline for producing rolling priv-

ilege logs. Plaintiff proposes that after any ESI production in which documents are withheld

based on privilege, the withholding party should provide a privilege log within 45 days. Dkt.

77 at 3. Defendant proposes that rolling privilege logs should be due 60 days after the cor-

responding production. Id. at 5.

       As Plaintiff notes, privilege disputes should be resolved promptly to avoid uncer-

tainty and the need to continue depositions. See id. at 3; see also AGT Civil Standing Order

§ VII.D (“Privilege logs must be promptly provided . . . .”). Defendant hasn’t identified any

concrete reason why it wouldn’t be able to abide by a 45-day deadline, other than its assertion

that discovery will be “highly asymmetrical.” Dkt. 77 at 5. The Court therefore adopts Plain-

tiff’s 45-day proposal. By August 5, 2026, the parties shall file for approval a proposed ESI

Order that conforms with this order.

13          Plaintiff’s Statement: This case is about Defendant Facebook’s systematic overcharging
14   of Facebook advertisers for several years between 2013 and 2017 (the “Class Period”) due to a
15   coding change in Facebook’s ad auction process that Facebook internally calculated to have caused

17   was widely understood by advertisers, Facebook’s advertising platform was supposed to employ
18   a type of auction in which the price of the winning bid for advertisement space on Facebook would
19   not be a factor influencing what the winning bidder would pay—i.e., a second price auction.
20   Consistent with this promise, Facebook told advertisers that it “only charges” advertisers “the bid
21   necessary to win the auction,” and recommended advertisers enter their “true maximum bid” based
22   on the assurance that the amount charged would not take into account what the winner of the
23   auction actually bid. ¶¶7, 34-39.1

13          Plaintiff’s Statement: This case is about Defendant Facebook’s systematic overcharging
14   of Facebook advertisers for several years between 2013 and 2017 (the “Class Period”) due to a
15   coding change in Facebook’s ad auction process that Facebook internally calculated to have caused
16   its advertisers to overpay by billions of dollars. Specifically, as Defendant’s contract provided and
17   was widely understood by advertisers, Facebook’s advertising platform was supposed to employ
18   a type of auction in which the price of the winning bid for advertisement space on Facebook would
19   not be a factor influencing what the winning bidder would pay—i.e., a second price auction.
20   Consistent with this promise, Facebook told advertisers that it “only charges” advertisers “the bid
21   necessary to win the auction,” and recommended advertisers enter their “true maximum bid” based
22   on the assurance that the amount charged would not take into account what the winner of the
23   auction actually bid. ¶¶7, 34-39.1

 3   bid. ¶¶74-84. After discovering this coding change—which Facebook internally calculated as
 4   resulting in billions of dollars in overcharges during the Class Period—Facebook did not inform
 5   or refund customers, but opted instead to keep the overcharge a secret. In fact, rather than disclose
 6   the change, Facebook internally decided to slowly fix the coding change and revert to the auction
 7   methodology that reflected a second price auction, which advertisers believed the Facebook
 8   platform employed. ¶¶88-92. In doing so, Facebook breached its implied and express contractual

Northern District of California

                                  13           Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness (herein “ITF”), a fitness company, brought this putative
                                  14   class action against Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (herein “Facebook,” Meta’s name
                                  15   prior to 2021), a social media company, alleging that Facebook overcharged advertisers
                                  16   over a five-year period. ITF alleges that Facebook promised to use a specific auction
                                  17   system called a second-price auction for pricing advertisements, but in 2013 secretly made
                                  18   a coding change that resulted in its use of a different auction system—one that was more
                                  19   expensive for advertisers. ITF brings claims for breach of contract, breach of California’s
                                  20   implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and violation of the California Unfair
                                  21   Competition Law (herein “UCL”).
                                  22   I.      AMBIGUITY
                                  23           At the May 15, 2026 motion hearing, Facebook urged the Court to dismiss ITF’s
                                  24   breach of contract claim. The Amended Complaint (herein “FAC”) alleges that the
                                  25   disputed language in the parties’ agreements required Facebook to run a second-price
                                  26   auction, and that it was this promise that Facebook breached. FAC (dkt. 47) ¶ 147. The
                                  27   Court first determines whether ITF’s interpretation of the contract is reasonable. See
                                  28   Trident Ctr. v. Conn. Gen. Life Ins. Co., 847 F.2d 564, 569 (9th Cir. 1988).
                                                                                      1
                                            Case 3:25-cv-03281-CRB       Document 72         Filed 05/26/26    Page 2 of 4




                                   1           The contractual language at issue appears on two pages in Facebook’s Help Center:
                                   2   a 2012 Help Center Page and a 2015 Glossary of Ad Terms (collectively, “the
                                   3   Agreements”).1 See FAC ¶¶ 104, 106. On those pages, Facebook promises to charge only
                                   4   the “minimum amount that you need to pay . . . which will sometimes be less than your . . .
                                   5   bid.” Id. ¶ 104. Facebook also instructs bidders to enter their “true maximum bid.” See
                                   6   id. ¶ 106.
                                   7           Facebook argues that ITF’s interpretation requiring Facebook to run a second-price
                                   8   auction is not reasonable. Mot. (dkt. 52) at 6. The Court agrees. The Court dismissed
                                   9   ITF’s original complaint because it failed to allege any contractual language requiring a
                                  10   second-price auction. See Tr. of Proceedings (dkt. 46) at 1. The FAC does not cure this
                                  11   deficiency, even considering the extrinsic evidence provided by ITF. See Trident Ctr., 847
                                  12   F.2d at 569 (“[T]he court must consider extrinsic evidence of possible ambiguity.”). The
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Agreements say nothing about auction types and only discuss auction pricing in vague
                                  14   terms. See FAC ¶¶ 104, 106.
                                  15           But the analysis does not end there, because ITF argues alternatively that the
                                  16   language in the Agreements is ambiguous. Opp’n (dkt. 53) at 9–10. If the “agreement is
                                  17   ambiguous, then interpretation of the agreement presents a fact issue that cannot be
                                  18   resolved on a motion to dismiss.” ASARCO, LLC v. Union Pac. R.R. Co., 765 F.3d 999,
                                  19   1008–09 (9th Cir. 2014).
                                  20           As discussed at the motion hearing, the Court disagrees with Facebook’s apparent
                                  21   contention that the plain language of the Agreements unambiguously grants Facebook
                                  22   limitless discretion to set its auction prices. And “[u]nder California law, the
                                  23   determination of whether a written contract is ambiguous is a question of law that must be
                                  24   decided by the court.” Brinderson-Newberg Joint Venture v. Pac. Erectors, Inc., 971 F.2d
                                  25   272, 278 (9th Cir. 1992) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).
                                  26
                                       1
                                  27     The Court takes judicial notice of the year on the 2012 Help Center and 2015 Glossary of Ad
                                       Terms webpages. See RJN (dkt. 55); Decl. (dkt. 54) Exs. 4–5; Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics,
                                  28   Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 999–1000 (9th Cir. 2018) (judicial notice for truth permissible where date “can
                                       be accurately and readily determined”) (internal quotation marks omitted).
                                                                                        2
                                            Case 3:25-cv-03281-CRB        Document 72        Filed 05/26/26     Page 3 of 4




                                   1           The Court concludes that the Agreements are ambiguous because there are at least
                                   2   two reasonable interpretations of their plain language. See Cachil Dehe Band of Wintun
                                   3   Indians of Colusa Indian Cmty. v. California, 618 F.3d 1066, 1080 (9th Cir. 2010) (court
                                   4   providing a reasonable interpretation of disputed terms after parties suggested
                                   5   interpretations that were not reasonable); Alexander Mfg., Inc. Emp. Stock Ownership
                                   6   Plan & Tr. v. Ill. Union Ins. Co., 560 F.3d 984, 988 (9th Cir. 2009) (identifying ambiguity
                                   7   after providing multiple interpretations of the contract); Admiral Ins. Co. v. Kay Auto.
                                   8   Distribs., Inc., 82 F. Supp. 3d 1175, 1180 (C.D. Cal. 2015) (district court providing its
                                   9   interpretation of a contract based on parties’ arguments).2
                                  10           The first reasonable interpretation is that the Agreements promise that the price that
                                  11   the auction winner pays will be independent of the price of the top bid. Under this
                                  12   interpretation, if the bid to beat in an auction was $9, a bidder could bid $10 or $500 and
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   pay the same final auction price. The interpretation is reasonable because the Agreements
                                  14   direct bidders to enter their “true maximum bid,” while promising to charge only the
                                  15   “minimum amount that you need to pay.” See FAC ¶¶ 104, 106. It is economically
                                  16   irrational to enter a “true maximum bid” in an auction unless the final price is independent
                                  17   of the price of the top bid. By contrast, if the price is dependent on the top bid, then
                                  18   bidders are disincentivized from placing a maximum bid, because the winner’s bid
                                  19   increases the price that the winner must pay. Further, language that the “amount you enter
                                  20   in the bid box is the maximum you’ll ever pay” could refer to unusual scenarios, including
                                  21   an auction with one bidder. See id. Consequently, a reasonable bidder could interpret the
                                  22   term “minimum amount that you need to pay” to mean that the price that the auction
                                  23   winner pays will be independent of the price of the top bid. See id. ¶ 104.
                                  24           The second reasonable interpretation is that the Agreements promise that the price
                                  25   that the auction winner pays will be dependent on the price of the top bid. Using the same
                                  26   example as above, Facebook would charge the bidder a higher final price if she bid $500
                                  27
                                       2
                                  28     The Court identifies those two reasonable interpretations in order to guide the parties going
                                       forward, not to offer a definitive interpretation of the Agreements.
                                                                                        3
                                            Case 3:25-cv-03281-CRB         Document 72         Filed 05/26/26      Page 4 of 4




                                   1   than if she bid $10. The interpretation is reasonable because the Agreements do not define
                                   2   the term “minimum amount that you need to pay” and other pricing terms. See id.
                                   3   Additionally, language that a bidder might pay her full bid supports the interpretation that
                                   4   Facebook has permission to make the price that the auction winner pays dependent on the
                                   5   price of the top bid.3 See id. ¶¶ 104, 106. Accordingly, a reasonable bidder could interpret
                                   6   the term “minimum amount that you need to pay” to mean that the price that the winner
                                   7   pays will be dependent on the price of the top bid. See id. ¶ 104.
                                   8           Because the Court may not resolve ambiguity in an agreement at the motion to
                                   9   dismiss stage, ITF’s breach of contract claim survives. See ASARCO, 765 F.3d at 1008–
                                  10   09.
                                  11   II.     CLAIMS
                                  12           Because the disputed agreement language is ambiguous, the Court DENIES
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Facebook’s motion to dismiss ITF’s breach of contract claim. Because ITF plausibly
                                  14   alleges that Facebook concealed overcharges from advertisers, its implied covenant claim
                                  15   is not duplicative of its breach of contract claim. See In re Facebook, Inc., Consumer Priv.
                                  16   User Profile Litig., 402 F. Supp. 3d 767, 792, 802 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (concealing
                                  17   distribution of user data sufficient to allege implied covenant claim). Consequently, the
                                  18   Court DENIES Facebook’s motion to dismiss ITF’s implied covenant claim. Because ITF
                                  19   fails to plead required information about its size, sophistication, and the relationship
                                  20   between its alleged contract with Facebook and the general public, see Grocery Outlet, Inc.
                                  21   v. Naftali, Inc., No. 23-cv-05254-CRB, 2024 WL 3540992, at *4 (N.D. Cal. July 24,
                                  22   2024), the Court GRANTS Facebook’s motion to dismiss ITF’s UCL claim with leave to
                                  23   amend within thirty days of this order should ITF wish to do so.
